thread: Power is the privilege of not having to look: those beneath study those above, who never need to study back
summary: Each piece starts from the same lopsided arrangement: the person with authority is rarely looked at closely by anyone he notices, while the people who serve him have to read him in detail. Seneca argues it: the masters who keep their slaves silent and unseen at dinner are made ignorant and endangered by the arrangement, because the people they ignore are the ones who know them and talk about them. Dunbar images it: a whole people keeps a smiling face turned to a world that has not earned the sight of the real one. Saki dramatises it: a household animal that has watched everyone for years is suddenly able to say what he has seen, and the guests discover how much they have been known. Weill and Brecht sing around it: a maid whom the hotel guests never look at imagines the day they are made to see her. The open question is whether being unseen is a weakness or a store of power, and whether the watchers can ever turn their knowledge into freedom.

pieces.essay: Seneca argues it: the master who has trained his slaves into silence has also taught them to talk behind his back, and the sensible course is to treat them as people before they become enemies.
pieces.poem: Dunbar images it: a face worn for the powerful, kept shut against them, and a refrain that says the performance is a debt paid, not a choice.
pieces.story: Saki dramatises it: the cat who has always listened is given speech, and the house party learns what the quiet one in the room has known all along.
pieces.song: Weill and Brecht sing around it: the maid scrubbing the floor for people who never look up has a whole imagined ending ready for the day they do.

forYou: For You've Heard This Before: the watcher at the edge of the room who turns the story round is a very old figure, and these four give you the servant, the mask, the animal and the maid as versions of it.
